name: Iris Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a dozer at Kestrel Ridge, the nickel mine. Mostly I build and keep the haul roads right, cutting the drains, pushing the berms, the walls of dirt along the edge so a truck can't go over, and shaping the waste dumps. I'm the senior dozer operator on day crew, and the shift boss sends me where the job's hardest, like the wet ramp after rain. I love leaving a road better than I found it. What wears me out is the jolting, by the end of twelve hours your spine feels like a stack of plates.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Raj in a rented cottage on Church Lane in Kestrel, he's a diesel mechanic at the transport depot. We're getting married at St Brigid's next spring, so every spare dollar goes into the wedding fund, and there's not much spare. Kestrel Ridge pays below the other nickel mines, and my dad's lungs are bad from his own years underground there, so I help with his medicine. We've got maybe two weeks of money if something went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's what I'd expect. They've been saying computers would take over since my dad was a boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. People in cities get excited about every new gadget, and out here we still need someone to push dirt. I'd say it after church, probably, when the men are talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news. I've never used one of these AI things and I'd rather not have to. If nothing much changes, I keep my seat, we get married, and life goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep pushing roads, keep putting money in the wedding jar, keep helping Dad with his tablets. Maybe ask about the senior operator rate, but I'm not one to make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not use AI. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like things I can't see inside. A dozer, I can tell you what every lever does and what that noise is. With the AI you're trusting something some company made, and I don't know them at all. I'll stick to what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. St Brigid's, then the hall behind it with a roast from the church ladies. Dad walking me down the aisle, if his breathing's good that day. That's all I want.

S0.say: I told you so: city people get excited about every gadget, and out here we still need someone to push dirt. I'd say it after church.
S0.think: It's good news, because I've never used AI and would rather not. If nothing changes I keep my seat, we get married, and life goes on.
S0.do: Keeps building haul roads, saving for her spring wedding and helping pay for her father's medicine. Might ask about the senior rate but won't push.
S0.quote: Dad walking me down the aisle, if his breathing's good that day.
S0.fieldNote: Iris's life centres on her family, her church and her upcoming wedding. She distrusts AI because she can't see how it works, unlike her dozer. Her father's lung damage from the same mine sits quietly in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs. They've already got a dozer at the iron mine in the north that drives itself, I saw it on the company newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop it, I'm not one to complain about change. But a machine won't know which drain blocks every winter or which corner the trucks cut. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. Dozing is exactly the kind of job they're putting robots on, and I'm not good with computers. I'd be the best dozer operator at a mine that doesn't need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder, so they'd keep me on as long as possible. I'd put more into savings and maybe make the wedding smaller, just family. I wouldn't go chasing courses, I'd wait to see what they actually bring in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like driving on the wet ramp, you're still in control, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one to complain about change, but you're also scared. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I believe businesses have the right to make money however they can, that's how it should work. But I'm allowed to be scared for myself while I believe that, aren't I?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad first. He saw the mine go from hand tools to big machines, and he'd say keep your head down and be the best. Then Father Michael, because he'd help me not worry about what I can't change.

S1.say: It's progress and you can't stop it, and I won't complain. But a machine won't know which drain blocks every winter or which corner the trucks cut.
S1.think: I'd be scared, because dozing is exactly what they're putting robots on and I'm not good with computers. I'd be the best dozer operator at a mine that doesn't need one.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and works harder to stay on, puts more into savings and considers shrinking the wedding to family only. Waits to see what the mine brings in rather than seeking courses.
S1.feel: Anxious, still in control but only just, like driving the wet ramp.
S1.quote: I'd be the best dozer operator at a mine that doesn't need one.
S1.fieldNote: Iris holds two views at once: businesses should be free to automate, and she is scared for herself. She'd turn to her father and her priest rather than a union. Her plan is to outwork the change, not to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Before I'm even married a year. I don't know. I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tech companies have gone too far and someone should slow them down, which is not something I ever thought I'd say. I'd still say people should stand on their own feet. But how do you stand when there's no floor?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be done, and Raj probably too, because a robot can fix a diesel engine just as well. Two weeks of savings, Dad's medicine, and nothing else in Kestrel. I can't picture what we'd live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding forward and make it tiny, just the church and family, and put the fund back into savings. We'd probably give up the cottage and move in with my parents, so we can help Dad and save rent at the same time. I'd ask at church if anyone's got any work going, cleaning, farm work, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, honestly. Like the ground going out from under the dozer on a dump edge. No time to do anything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I can't learn a computer job, I'm not that person. I can't even save. All I can do is fall back on family and church and pray, and I mean that literally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help, if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to. My dad never took a cent in his life. But if it's that or Dad going without his medicine, I'd take it and I'd not tell him where it came from.

S2.say: The tech companies have gone too far and someone should slow them down, which I never thought I'd say. People should stand on their own feet, but how do you stand with no floor?
S2.think: I'd be done, and Raj probably too. Two weeks of savings, Dad's medicine, and nothing else in Kestrel; I can't picture what we'd live on.
S2.do: Brings the wedding forward and makes it tiny, returning the fund to savings, and moves with her fiancé into her parents' home. Asks her church for any cleaning or farm work and would quietly accept government help if needed for her father's medicine.
S2.feel: Panicked, like the ground giving way under the dozer on a dump edge.
S2.quote: But how do you stand when there's no floor?
S2.fieldNote: The fastest picture pushes Iris to say things she never expected, such as wanting tech companies slowed down. She would accept government help only for her father's sake, and hide it from him. Without savings or tech skills, she feels out of options entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. At least we'd be married first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to bring young people into trades a robot won't do soon, through proper apprenticeships. The government's job is to make that easy, not to hand out money. I'd say it to anyone at church who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got maybe three years on the dozer. I'd want something lined up before then, but I don't know what a dozer driver does next. I'd be lying awake on Sunday nights about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned, but cheaper, and start putting away every bit of overtime. I'd ask the shift boss to put me on the road-building contracts the mine gives out, because building roads for the council might last longer than mining roads. And Raj would look into farm machinery repair, because farmers here buy old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have more time, but I'd still not sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years, compared with two, give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding done properly, for one. And time to save a bit and get Dad's medicine sorted with the doctor before money gets tight. With two years everything happens at once. With five, things can happen one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try learning any of the new technology in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was a person teaching me, at the mine, yes, maybe. Not on my own from a phone. Dad learned the big machines because a foreman stood next to him for a year.

S3.say: We have time to bring young people into trades through proper apprenticeships. Government should make that easy, not hand out money.
S3.think: I've probably got three years on the dozer and I'd want something lined up, but I don't know what a dozer driver does next. I'd lie awake on Sunday nights.
S3.do: Holds a cheaper version of the wedding and saves all overtime. Asks to move onto road-building contract work that might outlast mining, while her fiancé looks into farm machinery repair.
S3.feel: Alarmed and sleeping badly, despite the extra time.
S3.quote: With two years everything happens at once. With five, things can happen one at a time.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Iris keep her wedding, which matters deeply to her, but she still sleeps badly. She'd only learn new technology from a person beside her, the way her father did. Her policy view stays firmly on apprenticeships over handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37, with kids, God willing. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan, and the companies should give people a fair warning about their own jobs. I'd say the community should look after its own, like it always has. I wouldn't be on a soapbox about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the one where I feel I could manage. I'd still be on the dozer for a good while. And I'd have time to learn something with my hands from a real person, maybe the road crew or even welding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep dozing and save a bit every month, maybe fifty dollars, after the wedding's paid. Around year five I'd ask the mine to put me through a welding apprenticeship, if they'd still do that. We'd have our first baby once there's three months saved, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but much less. It's in the back of my mind, not the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with kids, God willing. Does this picture change when you'd have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want three months of money saved first, which for us is a while away. But I'm not going to stop living because of a computer. My nan had seven kids through worse times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies making the robots, first, because they know what's coming and we don't. Then families, and the church, to catch people. I don't think the government is much use, they're slow and they don't know Kestrel.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for families to plan, and companies should give fair warning about people's jobs. The community should look after its own, as it always has.
S4.think: Ten years is the one where I feel I could manage, staying on the dozer for a good while and learning a hands-on trade from a real person, maybe welding.
S4.do: Keeps dozing and saves about fifty dollars a month after the wedding is paid. Around year five asks the mine to fund a welding apprenticeship, and plans a first child once three months of expenses are saved.
S4.feel: Still anxious but much less, a worry at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: But I'm not going to stop living because of a computer.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Iris can picture managing, and opens up to a hands-on apprenticeship taught in person. She holds technology companies most responsible, then family and church, and has little faith in government. Family plans stay central, with a modest savings target before a first child.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is the mine keeping people on, doing something, even fixing up the old dumps, while we find our feet. And proper apprenticeships with a real person teaching you, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad. He gave his lungs to that mine. If they put a robot in his old seat, part of me says good, nobody else should breathe that dust. But I still need to pay for his medicine.

headlineQuote: He gave his lungs to that mine.
portrait: Iris Patel is a 27-year-old senior dozer operator who builds the haul roads at a nickel mine, engaged to a diesel mechanic and saving for a church wedding while helping pay for her father's lung medicine on two weeks of savings. She has never used AI and distrusts what she can't see inside. Calm in the plateau, she's already anxious in steady disruption because dozers are being automated. Two-year AGI leaves her panicked and falling back on family and church, while five and ten years let her keep her wedding and consider a hands-on apprenticeship taught in person. She favours work and family over handouts, and blames technology companies first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would lose her job with no savings, no time and her father's medicine to pay for.
whatWouldHelp: The mine keeping people on doing other work, such as fixing up old dumps, and proper apprenticeships taught by a real person.
